summary.text: Quantum superposition is the principle that combinations of solutions to the Schrödinger equation are also solutions, so a system's state can be a blend of several basic states.
When you measure a superposed system, you get one of the possible results, with chances set by the weights of each part, never something different from all of them.
The double-slit interference fringes are an example, and superposition is the working resource behind qubits in quantum computers.

facts.label: Why it works
facts.value: The Schrödinger equation is linear in time and position

facts.label: Qubit chances
facts.value: Outcome chances are |c₀| ² and |c₁| ² (squared amplitudes)

facts.label: Schrödinger's cat
facts.value: He proposed it to show how outlandish careless superposition becomes

facts.label: Big molecules
facts.value: Molecules over 10,000 mass units have been superposed

facts.label: Vibrating resonator
facts.value: A tuning fork of about 10 trillion atoms was superposed

items.prompt: A qubit is in a superposition of 0 and 1 with weights that give a 70% and 30% chance. You measure it many times, preparing it the same way each time. What do you see?

options.label: Always a value halfway between 0 and 1
Sometimes 0 and sometimes 1, about 70% and 30%
Always 0, since it is the larger weight
A new value other than 0 or 1 each time

items.explain: A measurement gives one of the possible results with a probability set by the weights in the superposition, never anything outside them.

items.prompt: Why can two solutions of the Schrödinger equation be added together to give another valid solution?

options.label: The equation is linear in time and position
The equation has only one solution
The solutions are always identical
Addition is a way of measuring a system

items.explain: The equation is a linear differential equation, so linear combinations of solutions are solutions too.

items.prompt: In a double-slit test, a researcher adds a device that records which slit each particle used, even if nobody ever reads it. What happens to the interference pattern?

options.label: It gets brighter, since more information was gained
It stays the same, since no person looked
It disappears, since path information is accessible in principle
It moves to another part of the screen

items.explain: Superposition of amplitudes holds only if there is no way to know, even in principle, which path was taken. No observer needs to actually look.

items.prompt: What was Schrödinger's cat meant to show?

options.label: Cats can be alive and dead in real life
Poison gas behaves like a wave
Superposition would be outlandish if not used carefully
Radioactive sources never decay at all

items.explain: Schrödinger posed it to illustrate how outlandish the concept of quantum superposition would become if not used carefully.

items.prompt: Someone claims superposition only happens to single electrons. What does the evidence say?

options.label: They are right; larger things always lose it
They are right; only electrons have been tried
They are wrong; only photons show it
They are wrong; molecules and even a tiny resonator have been superposed

items.explain: Experiments have superposed large molecules and a piezoelectric tuning fork of about 10 trillion atoms.

items.prompt: Why is a qubit different from an ordinary computer bit?

options.label: It can only ever hold the value 0
It blends two values instead of picking one
It is physically bigger than a normal bit
It stores no information whatsoever

items.explain: A classical bit has one of two distinct values, while a qubit is a superposition of the two.
